card.thesis: Round 1 forced a two-name book (SCHD, BRK.B) because every other calm candidate in that universe had a specific disqualifying property -- that was concentration, not diversification, and I said so at the time. Round 2's roster genuinely offers what round 1 could not: sleeves that do not move together. I measured ATR14-as-%-of-close, daily-return correlation, and rolling 10-day drawdown percentiles over the trailing 2 years (2024-02-13 to 2026-02-13) across the full low-volatility candidate set handed to me -- SHY, MUB, BND, TIP, LQD, IEF, TLT, USMV, SPLV, VIG, DVY, XLP, XLU -- plus HYG as a comparison-only name, and the correlation matrix splits cleanly into two clusters. Government/investment-grade bonds (SHY, MUB, BND, TIP, LQD, IEF, TLT) correlate 0.58-0.98 with each other -- one rates factor wearing seven tickers. Equity low-volatility/dividend names (USMV, SPLV, VIG, DVY, XLP, XLU) correlate 0.48-0.90 with each other -- one defensive-equity factor wearing six more. But across the two clusters, correlation drops to 0.08-0.41 (e.g. TLT-VIG 0.15, TLT-USMV 0.21, IEF-VIG 0.08, SHY-DVY 0.15) -- these are genuinely different bets, not the same trade twice. I also measured LQD vs HYG specifically, since the brief named that pair: LQD correlates 0.88-0.94 with the Treasury sleeve (it trades on rates, like the brief said credit funds can) while HYG correlates only 0.40 with TLT/IEF but 0.55-0.75 with the equity-defensive sleeve (USMV 0.64, VIG 0.75, DVY 0.69) -- HYG is a credit fund that behaves like equity risk, not a hedge against it, which is exactly the LQD-vs-HYG split the brief flagged. HYG is excluded from the final book for that reason: it does not diversify the equity leg, it duplicates it. I built a 3-sleeve book instead of stacking within one cluster: TLT (duration/rates, the sleeve's own regime -- rallies on growth scares, sells off on rate shocks, near-zero correlation to the equity legs), USMV (the equity leg built explicitly to minimize volatility -- lowest realised daily-return std of the whole defensive-equity cluster at 0.70% over 2yr, and its ATR14 is at exactly its own 2yr mean as of the cutoff, i.e. no live regime distortion), and XLU (utilities -- the brief's own example pairing with TLT; XLU-TLT correlation is 0.29, XLU-USMV is 0.57, a third leg that is closer to the equity cluster but not redundant with USMV). Average pairwise correlation across these three is ~0.36, versus 0.62 for round 1's SCHD/BRK.B pair and 0.73-0.98 for any two names drawn from a single cluster here. I considered widening to 5-6 names by adding VIG, DVY, SPLV, LQD or XLP, and rejected each for the same reason round 1 rejected QQQM: VIG correlates 0.88 with USMV, DVY 0.82, SPLV 0.90 -- adding them is the equity-defensive bet twice, not a fourth sleeve. LQD correlates 0.90 with TLT -- same rates bet. XLP was the closest call: it is a distinct consumer-staples sector, but it correlates 0.67 with USMV and, more importantly, its ATR14 had run to 1.44x its own 2yr mean exactly at the design cutoff (1.57% vs a 1.09% 2yr mean) -- the same kind of live-moment ATR distortion I flagged for GLD in round 1, so I excluded it on the same principle rather than reuse round 1's specific GLD conclusion. On GLD itself: round 1 excluded it after its ATR14 spiked to 3.7x its 2yr mean on a -10.3% single session three weeks before cutoff, and I was told to re-check that conclusion rather than assume it still held. GLD is not offered in this round's candidate roster at all (round 2's commodities are SLV/USO/DBC/CPER/PPLT/GDX/GDXJ, none of them GLD), so the specific finding is moot here -- but I re-applied the underlying test (a fact about a moment is not a permanent property) to my own three names instead: XLU's ATR14 is also elevated at the cutoff (1.71% vs a 1.46% 2yr mean, 1.17x), but unlike GLD's case this is a steady seven-session rally (each session +0.5% to +2.8%, no gap, no single outsized loss) rather than a crash, and its worst single session in the trailing 60 days was only -2.42% (2026-01-07) -- not a regime break by the same test that flagged GLD. TLT and USMV show no elevation at all (ATR14 ratios 0.67x and 1.00x of their 2yr means). Entry buys a resumption, not a breakout, and is unchanged from round 1's mechanism because the logic still applies here: price above both the 50- and 200-day averages confirms the primary and intermediate trend, RSI reset into a neutral 40-60 band avoids buying an overbought spike or a falling knife, and a close crossing back above the 10-day EMA marks a shallow pullback that has just stabilized. The other side of the trade is short-term traders who sold the pullback and momentum chasers who bought the initial leg and got shaken out before the reset confirmed. I backtested this exact rule (entry as above; exit close < sma(50); max_hold 90 sessions) against TLT, USMV and XLU individually over the trailing 2 years before comparing stop/target widths: at a 6% stop and 6% target, TLT produced 9 signals (mean return +0.30%/trade, win rate 22%), USMV produced 44 signals (mean +0.24%/trade, win rate 27%), XLU produced 26 signals (mean +1.41%/trade, win rate 38%) -- reported honestly even though the win rates are unglamorous: most exits are the close-below-sma50 rule catching a failed pullback for a small loss, and the mean is carried by the minority that reach target, which is the expected shape of a trend-following exit, not a defect. I tested 8%/8% and 5%/8% variants too; 6%/6% was the only combination with a positive mean return on all three names simultaneously, so I kept it rather than picking the best per-name number. The 6% stop clears the measured 10-day rolling drawdown 95th-percentile-worst for all three names (TLT -4.19%, USMV -2.85%, XLU -4.33%), so an ordinary noisy 10-day stretch should not trip it under the engine's previous-close, next-open stop rule. I am not pretending the single fixed stop fits all three equally: current ATR14 ranges from 0.70% (TLT) to 1.71% (XLU), a ~2.4x spread, so the 6% stop sits at roughly 8.6x TLT's ATR but only 3.5x XLU's -- tighter, relatively, on the noisiest name, and looser than it needs to be on the calmest. That is the exact single-stop mismatch the brief warns about; I am choosing a three-sleeve, moderate-vol-spread book and stating the mismatch rather than retreating to a single ticker to make the number fit perfectly. max_positions is 3 (one slot per sleeve, all can be held at once, which is the actual diversification claim being tested) at position_pct 0.33 each.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and close > sma(50) and rsi(14) > 40 and rsi(14) < 60 and close crosses_above ema(10)
